en: Composed by the Bhikṣu Huizhao of Dayun Monastery in Zizhou;
the second master’s commentary. The manas-consciousness is associated with all four types of feeling. Question:
Why is it that in the desire realm it is not associated with suffering [feeling], and why is it that up through the second dhyāna it is not concurrent with pleasant feeling?

The commentary has already finished its refutation. How [can it] be associated with sorrow or joy? Answer: For now, regarding its association with joy, there are three explanations. First, it is said that joy is associated with the sixth [consciousness].
Because the seventh [consciousness] coexists with the sixth,
why is it said to be associated with joy (*prīti*)? It is not so.
Why is this? It is because it is the result induced by wholesome karma belonging to the stage of "joyful application" (pramuditā-bhūmi) which takes [the first five sense objects] as its object;
it does not take the sixth [mental object] as its object. Therefore, this interpretation is incorrect. Second, it is because the fruit arises from the cause.
Alternatively, this eighth consciousness is induced by volition associated with the feeling of joy;

because the seventh [consciousness] takes this as its object—the fruit of projecting karma—it is called "taking that which has joy" and so forth, being accompanied by the feeling of joy. Third, it is said that they are accompanied because they are mutually concordant.
As it is said that the five consciousnesses take the preceding *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) as their object,
this aspect is produced from the perfuming (*vāsanā*) of the preceding five consciousnesses;
how then can the subsequent five consciousnesses be said to take the preceding aspect as their object?
This principle is likewise.
This fruit is summoned and brought about by joy (*prīti*) and its associated volition (*cetanā*);
although one contemplates this fruit because it accords with that cause, it is said to be "concomitant with joy."
The other three explanations regarding association with feeling (*vedanā*) should be understood by analogy with this.
The *Wenshu* (Commentary on the Questions) states:
"If all four feelings were present simultaneously, then the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*) would incur the fault of not being a sudden severance."
It is said that [the afflictions] are abandoned together with neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
Is it not the case that they are abandoned gradually because they are relinquished by changing the level (*bhūmi*)? The answer says: "If they were associated with joy (*prīti*) and so forth..."
The defiled dharmas must be abandoned in accordance with the distinctions of their respective stages,
just as in the case of the six consciousnesses; however,
if they are associated with the sensation of equanimity (upekṣā), they may be abandoned all at once.
Just as the eighth consciousness is abandoned all at once along with [the feeling of] equanimity,
this principle is fully established;
therefore, there is no fault.
Question: The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states that one takes the internal as an object and clings to it as "self.
Regarding this view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), does the term "view of self" refer exclusively to the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*)?

The self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) is also subsumed under the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*). Question: Even if they were both [included], what fault would there be? Answer: There is a fault in their being both.
If it is not called the view of self, then the same would apply to greed (*rāga*) and hatred (*dveṣa*).
That self-verifying portion (svasaṃvittibhāga) should not be greed and so forth;
if it is termed "self-view" (ātmadṛṣṭi),
one must admit that it takes external objects as its objective support.
Question: What is meant by "having the internal as its object"?

Should this not also be subsumed under invalid cognition (*apramāṇa*)? Answer: Only the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is called "self-view" (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), not the self-verifying-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*).
I see that self-realization is merely termed "defiled wisdom.
Why is it not the same as craving and so forth?
Answer: Craving and so forth can arise even when they are designated by their objects.

As in the case of [the self-cognition] co-arising with the five consciousnesses and so forth, because the view of self does not correspond to its object, self-cognition is not the view of self. Question: Why does it not correspond?

If it were not the view of self, it would merely be called defiled wisdom. Answer: Just as when taking the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) or other realms as objects, at the time the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) takes them as its object, they are not designated as "unconditioned" or "other realms."
However, the aspect of the perceiving subject (darśana-bhāga) is designated as having unconditioned objects and objects belonging to other realms;
the self-cognizing aspect (svasaṃvitti) cannot be so designated as having unconditioned objects and the like.
My view is also thus.
Furthermore, if seeing its own essence is what constitutes the view of self (ātma-dṛṣṭi), then it is established.
If, however, the view of self were defined by taking a self as its object,
then self-cognition would not be such a view.
The same applies to greed and the other afflictions.
If greed arises taking form as its object, it is designated as "greed" and so forth;
however, this is not the case for self-cognition itself.
Because it does not take form as its object,
and because greed is self-verified, it is called "greed" and so forth;
its own essence is likewise [so named].
Regarding this treatise, as for why this [state] corresponds exclusively to the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*):
the question is, when the seventh [consciousness] takes the eight [objects] as its conditions,
it corresponds exclusively to the feeling of equanimity according to those conditions.
The sixth [consciousness] takes the seventh and eighth as its objects;
it is accompanied by equanimity alone. Answer: The seventh [consciousness] always internally takes [its own] objects;
it is accompanied by equanimity alone according to the circumstances.
The sixth [consciousness] takes both internal and external objects as its conditions;
it cannot be exclusively associated with equanimity. Question: These six [consciousnesses] are the projectors, and the seventh is the projected.
Accordingly, by following those projectors, [the seventh] becomes untainted (*anāsrava*).
The seven [mental factors] are those that are induced, while the six are those that induce.
It should follow that the inducing factors are associated with all three types of sensation. Answer: When the untainted (anāsrava) arises, it is difficult [to categorize];
however, when arising in dependence on another, it is untainted.

Because it always functions spontaneously with respect to its object, it does not admit of the three types of feeling. Question: Why is it that the seventh [consciousness], though produced by uncontaminated [factors] or induced by others, does not follow the inducing factors in admitting the three types of feeling?
The seventh [type of] untainted [attainment] is induced by another;
it does not follow the same level as that which induces it. Answer: When pure dharmas arise, it is difficult [to maintain otherwise];
they follow the same level as that which induces them.
Equanimity arises spontaneously;

it does not follow the inducing [karma] and is common to all three feelings. Question: Why does the seventh consciousness arise spontaneously and not follow the inducing [karma], being common to all three feelings?
The five consciousnesses arise spontaneously;

they do not follow the leading [mental factors] and thus do not correspond to all three types of feeling. Answer: Because the five consciousnesses easily detach and arise, they follow other [factors] and correspond to all three types of feeling.

The seventh [mental consciousness] takes a single category as its object and does not follow the other three feelings. Question: Since the five consciousnesses arise spontaneously and are induced by others, they should follow their inducers and thus pertain to all three feelings.

The seventh category, that which is induced by others, should follow its inducer as being associated with all three types of sensation. To this, the substantive answer states: although the five sensory consciousnesses are induced by others, they are not associated with vitarka and vicāra, which are the inducers.
Although equanimity is induced by other factors,
it does not follow those inducers in being associated with the three types of sensation.
As for the treatise’s statement, "If it were different from the ālayavijñāna," and so forth:
The *Yaoji* (Essential Compendium) states:
Some say that because the three stages of "having explained" (*youshuo*) and "having understood" (*youjie*) do not exist, there is no sense of "constant revolution" (*hengzhuan*).
This, too, is unreasonable.
Because it has not been severed and continues to arise constantly, it is—
just like the eighth consciousness— always termed *ālaya* until one enters the four stages [of the path].
Therefore, based on this interpretation, it is said that it exists but is not mentioned [as such].
Alternatively, one might argue that it is not stated because it is identical [to the preceding].
We say this is not so. Even if the ālayavijñāna enters the four stages, it is said to "perpetually evolve" because it has not yet become untainted (anāsrava).
It is not said that it constantly revolves like a stream by way of its name;
because the three states of the manas transform into the untainted (anāsrava),
this transformation is not constant, and thus it is not like a stream.
Treatise:
Under which nature are this mind and its mental factors subsumed?
The Commentary provides two interpretations.
At the beginning, it is said that there are paired questions and paired answers.
Because the King is constituted by the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) of the mind,
the King who is manifested is first presented.
Therefore, the treatise states:
"Because these four afflictions associated with this manas are defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*),
it subsequently reveals that [the manas] is obscured (*nivṛta*) by virtue of being constituted by those kings."
The treatise states: "Because this is the subtle basis for these concomitant defiled phenomena, both [questions] are posed and answered.
Question: Do the seven [mental factors] take the eight [objects] as a self, or do they follow each object according to its respective realm-bound nature?
Regarding the sixth [type of craving], which takes the three realms as its object and is bound by the fetters of the three realms: Answer: They mutually increase within their own respective levels;
they are bound according to their own specific level.
They do not increase across different levels.
It is not bound by other stages.
Treatise:
This refers to the defiled manas in this state.

The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states that this applies to both types of grasping (*dvividha-grāha*). The *Yāojí* (Essential Collection) and other works state that it refers exclusively to the grasping of a person (*pudgala-grāha*).
I do not speak of attachment to dharmas.
Why? Because if one speaks of attachment to dharmas, [it would be a contradiction].
For what reason does the treatise state that the noble paths of the three vehicles possess the meanings of "suppression" (*vāsanā*) and "extinction"?
Furthermore, it states that those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) of the two vehicles should not permanently abandon [the afflictions].
Moreover, this is the explanation of Dharmapāla.
The three types of non-existence are explained based on the *kliṣṭamanas* (afflicted mind).
Therefore, it is known that the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) is not termed the *kliṣṭamanas*.
This means that [our position] merely accords with what is stated in the treatises and does not contradict them.
Because this is its fundamental nature,
although the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas of fixed lineage cannot subdue or sever it,
it is not termed "defiled mind" (kliṣṭamanas) when viewed from their perspective, as it is not defiled for them.
Regarding those of indeterminate lineage and those fixed in the Mahāyāna,
attachment to phenomena (dharma-grāha) is termed defilement;
however, even the noble path of the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā) cannot suppress it in those of indeterminate lineage.
Therefore, the treatise states that the noble paths of the three vehicles possess the meanings of both suppression and eradication.
If it were merely the grasping at a self,
one should say that the noble paths of all three vehicles are equally capable of suppressing and eradicating it.
Why must it be said that they exist?
There is no fault in asserting that these three stages are non-defiled;
for attachment to dharmas, when viewed in relation to those of the two vehicles with fixed natures, is not termed "defiled."
It is not non-existent within the three stages;
however, if one considers it in relation to the Bodhisattva, it does not exist within those three stages.
The phrasing is inclusive while the meaning remains implicit.
The rest are not all [included].
The treatise says:
Furthermore, it is like a person who has not yet realized [the truth].
The *Ximing Liang* states:
"If the emptiness of phenomena has not yet arisen,
there must be a constant functioning of the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*)."
Because the antidote has not yet arisen, it is like the state of self-grasping; thus, the thesis established in this example is unproven.
The *Shuyao* states:
In the stage where attachment to phenomena has not yet realized the emptiness of phenomena,
there must be a phenomenon that is constantly active,
because it is subsumed under one or the other of the two attachments.
It is just like the grasping at birth; there is a false claim that it is a fallacy because it contradicts the intrinsic nature (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the property-possessor (*dharmin*).
This is a mistaken citation of the essential points, for both the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*) established in the commentary on the *Vigrahavyāvartanī* are subject to fault.
Question: Regarding one who dwells in the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), does the Blessed One enter the absorption of cessation?
Answer: There are three interpretations.
First, it is said that he does not enter [the meditative absorption]. If this is so, how can he be endowed with all the qualities?
The answer is: he has attained the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), yet it does not manifest. Second, it is said that he does enter.
If that is so, for what reason is the entry [of a bodhisattva] rebuked?
Answer: It is those who are addicted to pleasure who are rebuked.

Furthermore, there are also various sūtras that encourage bodhisattvas to enter [the meditative attainments]. Question: Once one has entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the six consciousnesses do not function.
"How is it possible to benefit sentient beings? Answer: "By means of the power of preparatory application (*prayoga*) and the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*).
[The Buddha] manifests majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*) while not arising from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

The Buddha does this spontaneously (*anābhoga*), without relying on preparatory application. Third, it is said that although it appears as if he has entered [the absorption], in reality he has not entered. According to tradition:
The *Sāgaramati-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states that when one enters the meditative absorption of the cessation of principles (*tattva-nirodha-samādhi*), consciousness does not function;
however, when one enters the meditative absorption of the cessation of phenomena (*vastu-nirodha-samādhi*), consciousness still arises.

What is described as "resembling entry" refers precisely to the meditative absorption of the cessation of phenomena. Nevertheless, among the three interpretations found in the transmitted texts, the second interpretation is superior.
Therefore, this objection is raised:
if the wisdom of equality (samatājñāna) were to rely upon the sixth consciousness, it would necessarily be subject to interruption;
for it is admitted that the Buddha’s activity is constant, like the mirror-like wisdom (ādarśajñāna).
If [the mind] does not enter cessation, or even if it enters but does not cease,
how could the six constant mental activities (ṣaḍ-ābhoga-nitya-carita) constitute a difficulty?
To say so would mean that both the thesis (pakṣa) and the reason (hetu) established would be faulty.
The Commentary states: "Regarding the 'contradictory certainty' (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) concerning its own dharma and its own characteristic, one modifies that reason by stating:
'excluding the mental consciousness associated with the Noble Path, etc.'"
It lacks a simultaneous support (sahabhū-āśraya),
because it is a mental consciousness (manovijñāna), just like the mental consciousness in the three states [of non-conception, sleep, and fainting].
Because of this, it is revised from what preceded.
The preceding reason should also be excluded because it is subsumed under the three stages and the six consciousnesses;
thus, there is no fallacy of uncertainty.
The *Shuyao* states:
Furthermore, there is a contradiction with the self-characteristic of its own dharma,
because the non-learner’s indeterminate mind is taken as the "dharma of similar kind" (*sadharmya*).
The meaning of this authoritative statement is as follows:
since those beyond training (aśaikṣa) never possess the seventh [consciousness],
it is called "indeterminate" (aniyata).
Except for those in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), where the sixth consciousness does not exist;
this is because the sixth mental consciousness at the time of entering cessation is taken as the "homogeneous factor" (*sadharmya*).
However, according to the principles of reasoning:
Within this, there are two propositions:
first, the general establishment of the sixth consciousness;
second, the exclusion of three states to select the remaining sixth consciousness.
The causes are also twofold:
first, the general cause, because they are subsumed within the six consciousnesses;
second, the specific cause, which distinguishes three stages from those that are not three stages.
The remaining [minds] are subsumed under the six consciousnesses;
as appropriate, each is established as two positions by means of two causes.
This can be understood through reflection.
Treatise:
First, it pervades the continuums of all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Regarding this, there are two explanations from Ximing.
First, it clarifies the attachment to continuity;
second, it states that "continuity" refers to the body.
The *Yaoji* (Essential Collection) also says: [as cited above].
This refers to the continuity of what is designated as the body of the five aggregates;
it is neither the grasping [of a self] nor the mind. Now, we say this is not so;
the meaning of this passage is to reveal that there is continuity with intervals between the three stages.
First, this is explained in general terms;
subsequently, it is further analyzed regarding the times when [the mind] arises and does not arise.
Therefore, the preceding section concerns continuity.
This clarifies that the mental faculty (*manas*) associated with these [states] is both interrupted and continuous,
but does not clarify its physical body (*kāya*).
If the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are taken as the basis, it is called "continuity."
Furthermore, since the grasping at a self also relies upon the bodies of noble ones,
why do you not say it is "continuous"?
Likewise, the wisdom of equality also relies upon bodhisattvas.
Why, then, does the treatise not speak of "continuity"?
Although the functions of the two views— of self and of dharmas— are distinct, they both rely upon the same wisdom.
The *Yāojí* (Essential Compendium) and other texts state:
"There is certainly no separate category of cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that is fixed;
this has already been briefly explained above."
Now, this shall be further clarified:
If there were no distinct seeds, when Arhats and others give rise to the grasping of dharmas (*dharmagrāha*), would they be able to perfuse seeds?
If you say they do not perfuse them, [then how can such grasping arise]?
Since the four conditions for being an active perfumer (*bhāvakatva*) are incomplete, why would it not fail to perfume?
If you claim that it does indeed perfume,
would this not then constitute a separate seed?
The perfuming agent is exclusively the cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa). Furthermore,
it is stated that the function of a single wisdom is divided to perfume and form two kinds,
which are distinct seeds.
As for the question of why it is necessarily stated that they are afflictions (*kleśa*),
this is based on their fundamental nature and because they constitute the majority.
Treatise.
Regarding the "mind associated with the attachment to dharmas" (dharmagrāha-samprayukta-manas), the phrase "and so forth" (etc.
regarding the two vehicles includes ordinary beings;
that is, both those of the two vehicles and ordinary beings. Ximing and others say:
It encompasses the bodhisattva’s knowledge of the emptiness of persons;
because it does not obstruct that knowledge, it is also called "non-defiled. The *Yaoji* (Essential Compendium) states that the latter explanation is superior.
If ordinary beings and bodhisattvas are equal in this regard, why are they not identical?
We reply that the former is superior.
The treatise states that among bodhisattvas, both ordinary and noble ones are included.
If one expects that a bodhisattva is undefiled by the emptiness of arising,
then at the moment when the emptiness of arising arises, they would not be a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, one should also say that for all bodhisattvas, even the wisdom of the emptiness of arising is called "defilement."
The preceding sentence provides a general statement,
and its wording does not exclude [the bodhisattva].
Therefore, we know that when viewed generally, it is not equal to the time when a bodhisattva gives rise to the realization of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
However, regarding the Bodhisattvas, the term "equal" is not explicitly stated,
because it is subsumed within the word "all," and because the latter serves as a reflection of the former.
Neither [position] is at fault.
Regarding the argument that [this consciousness] is subsumed under "that which is born of maturation" (*vipākaja*),
it is, for instance, like the mind born of maturation up to the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa*).
Regarding the distinction between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna:
in the Hīnayāna, the four meditative states (*citta-samādhi*) are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
However, the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*) pertains to both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The mind of deportment (*airyāpathika*) is broad;
it is not subsumed by the other three [minds].
It enters into deportment exclusively as a single category and not as a pair. Question: Do the initiations such as receiving the precepts (*śīla*) give rise to the mind of deportment?
"Is this not wholesome? Answer: According to the intent of that school, the mind that desires to receive the precepts is wholesome;
the arising of prostrations and so forth is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
However, the establishment of the essence of the precepts does not depend on the volition that initiates bodily or vocal karma;
rather, it is established based on form and sound.
In the Mahāyāna, transformations arise solely from the four dhyānas.
They pertain to the wholesome, the indeterminate, and both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*).
As for the remaining three, they pertain to all three natures— wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate— as well as the tainted and untainted,
as has already been explained previously.
However, they may arise in combination.
For example, like walking on a road while singing, dancing, and beating a drum;
or, minds arising before and after may also occur simultaneously.

Alternatively, karmic-resultant minds cannot arise simultaneously; however, non-karmic-resultant minds, as well as wholesome and unwholesome minds, can—this is the meaning explained regarding the four types of mind.
It is not that multiple minds arise concurrently.
As the *Mahā-śāstra* states: "This exists conventionally."
It is said that they are "indeterminate" (avyākṛta) based on a specific explanation.
Regarding the treatise’s discussion of mind (citta), thought (manas),
and consciousness (vijñāna), the Sarvāstivādins state:
The five gates have distinct meanings.
The first is the gate of names,
which simply applies the name "giving."
From the perspective of two meanings: that which gathers and gives rise [to phenomena] is called mind (*citta*);
that which discerns is called consciousness (*vijñāna*);
and that which cogitates is called intellect (*manas*).
Regarding the gate of the functions of the three karmas:
that which is known from afar is called *citta* (mind),
and that which opens and guides is called *manas* (intellect).
That which undergoes rebirth is called consciousness (*vijñāna*).
In terms of the four temporal dimensions,
that of the past is called mind (*manas*).
In the present, it is called "mind" (*citta*);
in the future, it is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*); and within the aggregates (*skandha*), it is called "consciousness. This is from the *Pañcavastuka-vibhāṣā*.
When situated in the bases (*āyatana*), it is called "mind" (*manas*); when situated in the realms (*dhātu*), it is called "consciousness" (*citta*.
Both terms apply universally to all six consciousnesses.
There is no mind or thought apart from the six external objects;
this is confirmed by examining the textual commentary.
In the Mahāyāna, however, they are distinct.
Regarding the *Vimokṣa-sūtra*,
some say it is called a *Vimokṣa-sūtra* because one attains liberation by severing hindrances through the Path.
The *Yaoji* (Essential Compendium) states:

"Since works such as the *Devaparipṛcchā-sūtra* are not classified as *vimokṣa-sūtras* (liberation sūtras), [the opponent argues that this text is not the Buddha’s word]. I now say: This is not so. For what sūtra does not enjoin the cultivation of the path to sever hindrances?
If it were not so, how could one claim that because it "induces the application of remedies" (*pratipakṣa*), it is clearly the Buddha’s teaching?
Therefore, what was stated previously is correct.
However, "The Questions of Devaputra" is a specific title.
As for the term "liberation" (vimukti):
This is the general designation for those who do not enter into the Āgamas.
Regarding the statement that "the defiled mind (kliṣṭa-manas) is constant," the various schools offer differing interpretations.
Furthermore, the Vaibhāṣikas say:
"The afflicted mind refers to the sixth consciousness."
Regarding "at all times" (*nityakāla*):
it is not called "at all times" because it is uninterrupted,
as in the cases of "constantly giving food" or "constantly experiencing pleasure."
Regarding "arising and ceasing together":
it does not mean that they are simultaneous to be called "together";
rather, they are called "together" because arising and ceasing both exist simultaneously.
That is to say, all doubts possess arising and ceasing;
as for one who is liberated,
the path of counteraction arises.
Regarding the statement "it neither existed in the past nor will exist in the future":

this means that while its acquisition (*prāpti*) has been relinquished and it is freed from the bonds of conditions, it is not without an essential nature (*svabhāva*). The Sthavira school says: [as follows].
The defiled mind is constant;
that is to say, the subtle mental consciousness,
because it is uninterrupted.
Regarding those that are co-nascent, they are said to perish together.
Because the past and future do not exist, they are neither what has already occurred nor what is yet to be. Question:
If the subtle mental consciousness, like feeling and so forth, is constantly continuous and co-nascent with the four [mental factors], how can it be so?
The second chapter of the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* asks: "How so?
Because it is based on defilement and because its continuity is uninterrupted.
This is raised as an objection; furthermore, according to the ninefold cycle of consciousness (*navacittavartana*), the *bhavanga*-consciousness is the consciousness at the moment of rebirth.
It is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Furthermore, the lower section of the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"In the Avīci Hell, there is that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*)."
This is the meaning of the Sthavira school.
Based on this, it is not a subtle defiled mental consciousness that undergoes rebirth;
thus, it should not be [considered] their interpretation. Answer: Within the Sthavira school, there are both fundamental and derivative positions.
The view that the unobscured [mind] undergoes rebirth is the fundamental position;
the view that the subtle defiled mind undergoes rebirth is the derivative position.
Among the Sautrāntikas as well, there are both fundamental and derivative positions.
The interpretation of the sūtra follows this principle.
To clarify non-common ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*),
the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (She lun), fascicle 5, states:
This cannot be said to exist in the five consciousnesses,
because there is no antidote present in those locations. Where an antidote exists, [it may be said to exist].
There is that which is to be remedied here;
it is not within the five consciousnesses that the remedy exists, because the Path of Seeing does not arise therein.
This means that during the stage of the Path of Seeing, the five consciousnesses have not yet become untainted (*anāsrava*).
If there were a unique ignorance (āveṇikī avidyā),
it would also be termed "intoxication" even during the stages of the noble ones (ārya),
which would contradict the teaching.
This is because it speaks of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*);

it does not say that noble ones (*ārya*) also constantly give rise to them. Furthermore, this is stated with reference to a bodhisattva’s arising of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), at which time the seventh [consciousness] is also untainted (*anāsrava*).
This does not refer to the path of vision (darśanamārga) arising in those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), nor is it because the seventh [consciousness] is established as the sixth. Question:
Since those of no nature (*abhāva*) lack any remedy (*pratipakṣa*), they should altogether be non-existent. Answer: Because they are ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Furthermore, the intent of this objection is based on the arising of the path of seeing (darśanamārga) for those who possess a lineage (*gotra*).

Otherwise, if one were to allow that the five aggregates constitute the knowledge of what has been accomplished (*kṛtāvijñāna*), there would have to be an "unshared" [defect]. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* further states:
Nor does it exist within the afflicted mental consciousness (*kliṣṭa-manovijñāna*),
because when it is associated with other afflictions,
the designation "unshared ignorance" (*āveṇikī avidyā*) would not be established. This being so, how could it coexist with the four [afflictions]?
The first master’s position should be accepted as superior. In response, that treatise presents the following objection:
"Non-associated ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*) is also not established [in all states], because it is always associated with the view of a self-body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and other such afflictions."
The author himself explains:
"Your objection is unjust.
It is not my intention to say that it is called 'unshared' (āveṇika) because it is dissociated from other afflictions."
However, it is said that because these [mental factors] do not exist in others or in other locations, they are called "unshared" (*āveṇika*),
just like the eighteen unshared qualities of a Buddha (*aṣṭādaśāveṇikabuddhadharma*).
As for what was stated previously— that being associated with other afflictions is termed "non-attainment"— [it refers to the following].

This is because one observes what others have established in order to reveal their faults. This intention addresses other schools, such as the Sarvāstivādins, by stating that [a fault] shared with others is not called "unshared" (asādhāraṇa), thereby demonstrating their self-contradiction;
it is for this reason that the objection is raised.
It is not that what I have taught is not called "unshared" because it occurs simultaneously with others.
Regarding the treatise:
"If this consciousness did not exist, how could that basis exist?"
In the Mahāyāna, it is revealed that if the seventh consciousness did not exist, the meaning of the sūtras would not be established.
Therefore, the objection is raised against the outsider:
"The eye and so forth are included herein; together with the simultaneously arising faculties, they are called the two conditions."
The mental faculty (*manas*) is also included within the six [faculties].
Accordingly, one should rely on the present mental faculty as being designated by two conditions. An external critic challenges the Mahāyāna, saying:
"The mental consciousness arises from two conditions."

If it is argued that [a faculty] cannot arise based on two conditions because it lacks intentionality (*anabhisandhi*), what prevents two conditions from giving rise to a sense-faculty even though it lacks intentionality?
This fault is shared by the Sautrāntikas, as they likewise accept this; thus, there is no such error.

This objection is raised because it is admitted that [a cognition] can arise even with respect to what is non-existent. Answer: Possession (*prāpti*) and its own non-possession (*aprāpti*) are both dharmas.
A present manifestation arises from two conditions, including one that has no object.
When the past mind has ceased, the present [object] does not exist.

If the faculty of mental consciousness does not arise, it would be untenable; however, if one follows the Sarvāstivāda school from the perspective of the Mahāyāna tenets, this same objection can be raised.
For the Sautrāntika school, since cessation is non-existent, they merely employ the conventional designation "mental consciousness."
Regarding the great difficulty, it is said:
For the five consciousnesses, the six [objects] and the two [types of] conditions are real roots and also real;
for the mental consciousness, the six [objects] and the two [types of] conditions are provisional roots and also provisional.
However, what follows is a specific refutation of the Sautrāntika school;
this is first presented as a hypothetical statement to serve as the objection raised by the Vaibhāṣikas.
Furthermore, according to the Mahāyāna, it is answered that the root-dharmas are the basis (*āśraya*).

Non-attainment (*aprāpti*) is merely a conceptual construct associated with the mind. Moreover, it is explained that the characteristic of being "proximate" (*sākṣāt*) is that which is dependently originated;
even the absence of a substance (*avastu*) is real.
The same applies to the five and six [consciousnesses] regarding their two conditions;
the sense organs that serve as their bases do not depend on external objects.
Furthermore, it is difficult to explain how the Sūtra speaks of "six pairs of conditions."
If the sense faculties were merely provisional, consciousness would not arise;
consciousness relies upon the six pairs of conditions.
If objects were merely provisional, [consciousness] should not arise. Answer: The power of the object-condition is remote.
If it is granted that consciousness arises through designation,
then its basis, its predominant condition,
its force, and its proximity would not arise through designation.
However, since the objective part (*nimittabhāga*) is similar to the sense faculty (*indriya*) in its actual manifestation, it ought to be considered "good.
It cannot be said that visible form (*rūpa*) is the supported (*āśrita*).
[The author] refutes the Sthavira school as follows:
The five consciousnesses rely on the material sense organs;
the five consciousnesses are without conceptual discrimination.
The mental consciousness relies on the material sense organs.
The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is non-conceptual.
When challenged regarding the Mahāyāna, it is said:
"The eighth [consciousness] relies upon the mind-faculty (*manas*)."
Question: The eighth [consciousness] is non-conceptual;
what prevents the sixth [consciousness], which relies on the material sense organs, from being conceptual?
Answer: The nature of material phenomena (rūpa-dharma) is dull.
Fifth, regarding non-discrimination: the mental faculty (*manas*) is the predominant basis for it, for discrimination occurs only through volition (*cetanā*).
An external objection states that there are six bases for discrimination, corresponding to the six sense faculties.
Regarding the eight [consciousnesses] that rely on the mental faculty (*manas*), eight possess discrimination. Answer: The eighth [ālayavijñāna] lacks clarity by its very nature;
although it relies on the mental faculty, it does not discriminate.
The sixth [consciousness], however, possesses manifold capacities by its very nature.
Furthermore, it is distinguished by virtue of being the basis for the mind (*manas*).
Question: Why is that which is present called "mind" (*manas*), while the name "mind" is established based on that which has already ceased?
The present is also called consciousness (*vijñāna*).
That which has already ceased and serves as a basis for the present should also be called consciousness. Answer: The term "mind" (*manas*) applies to two meanings.
That which has already ceased and serves as a support acquires the name "mind."
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is merely the act of discerning.
That which has already ceased lacks this capacity and is therefore not called consciousness.
Treatise.
Regarding the phrase "due to the grasping of self, it causes [the afflictions] to arise within the six consciousnesses," the commentary offers two interpretations;
the latter interpretation is correct.
Ximing adopts the former;
the Yaoji does the same.
I, however, maintain that the latter explanation is superior.
Because of the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*), one cannot eliminate the appearance [of a subject] and say, "I am able to practice giving.
How could the seventh consciousness (*kliṣṭa-manas*) give rise to the thought "I am able to give" by taking giving and so forth as its object?
Therefore, this is the intended meaning of the original commentary.
This is the sixth self.
It becomes more clearly manifest by relying upon the seventh self as its basis;
it is not that the one who thinks "I give" is the seventh self.
If one holds that the characteristics of the three spheres constitute the seventh self,
then since these are not always subdued even prior to the seventh stage, how much less so before the stages?
Since they cannot be subdued [prior to the stages], [the seventh self is not eliminated].
Because the three wheels of giving and so forth are able to eliminate signs,
it is said that there are two kinds of "bondage of signs."
The first [ignorance] has all aspects;
by means of the seventh [consciousness],
it grasps the aspects of the three wheels through the two types of self-clinging.
Although the sixth [consciousness] is also explained by means of the seventh,
the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*— relying on its basis—
states that it refers to itself as "I" when one thinks, "I am able to practice giving and so forth."
It is not that the grasping at a self, which follows from ignorance, can be separated [from it];
nor do ignorance and the other afflictions exist apart from their basis.
If one were to claim that this seventh [consciousness] is the grasping at a self, its characteristic would still not be eliminated.
One should say that it is not possible to grasp the signs and so forth apart from the self-grasping nature of ignorance;
why, then, must one say that it is not apart from the persistence of the self-grasping of ignorance?
This explains the reason by stating that it is not apart from its basis; it does not state that they are identical.
However, when this treatise cites the *Yogācārabhūmi* as proof,
it does so as a general authority;
it is not intended solely to prove the characteristics of those three wheels.

If it were said that only by means of untainted (anāsrava) non-conceptual [wisdom] can these signs be suppressed, then prior to the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga), they would not constitute the *pāramitās*.

This is because the tainted preparatory (*prayoga*) non-conceptual wisdom cultivated prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) is capable of suppressing the sixth [consciousness], thereby fulfilling the definition of *maitreya* (the state of being "loving" or "beneficent"). Thus, the question asks: "What is meant by 'bondage by signs' (*nimittabandhana*)?"
Is it the afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*)?
Is it the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)? Answer: Even if that were so, what fault would there be? There are faults in both cases.
If it were by way of the afflictive obstruction...
In the state of the contaminated mind of those in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) of the two vehicles, there should be no bondage by signs,
because the grasping at a self has been severed.
If [bondage] were due to the cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa), [then this would follow].

The subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhābhisamaya*) regarding the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) should be bound by signs (*nimitta-bandhana*). There are two explanations: first, it is said that this is due to the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). If that were so, then the subsequently attained [knowledge] regarding the emptiness of persons would also be bound. The answer is: because they are not concordant.

According to Sthiramati’s commentary, this [explanation] is correct. Second, it is said that the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) constitute the nature of the bondage of signs (*nimittabandhana*). If that were so, then the tainted wholesome and indeterminate minds of those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) among the two vehicles would lack the bondage of signs. The answer is: because the substance of these objective parts (*nimittabhāga*) is itself tainted (*sāsrava*).
This is because it is the seeds induced by that [grasping at a self] which have been perfumed and formed;
thus, although the substance of that grasping at a self has now been severed and exhausted, [the afflictions] still persist due to the presence of the fetters of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*).
However, the substance of grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) is not itself the primary fetter of signs.
Because it grasps at signs, it serves as a basis for the arising of that self-grasping;
thus, it is an auxiliary to the bondage of signs.
This refers to the non-learner’s (aśaikṣa) scattered wholesome states and the indeterminate mind.
There is also this assistance for those who have not yet abandoned the bonds of characteristics;
although there is such assistance in the subsequently attained wisdom of the emptiness of persons,
it lacks the "characteristics" and "true characteristics" that were previously perfumed by outflows and constitute the actual bonds.
Therefore, it can be said that they do not exist;

this explanation is correct. However, the grasping at the characteristics of the three wheels belongs exclusively to the sixth consciousness, whereas the fifth and eighth [consciousnesses] operate spontaneously (*anābhoga*).
Seventh, because of internal conditions:
if there are outflowing marks (*sāsrava-nimitta*), they are called the "bondage of marks" (*nimitta-bandhana*).
This applies to all eight consciousnesses. Question: Various treatises state only that it prevents the six consciousnesses from being able to extinguish marks.
How is it that what is now explained applies to all eight consciousnesses? Answer: That is based on the three wheels [of agent, object, and action].
Because the sixth consciousness clings to a self, it causes all six consciousnesses to be constrained by appearances and fail to realize they are illusory.
The seventh [type of] object conditions the eight as well, because they are bound by signs;
since they are fundamentally bound by signs,
they are all bound by signs.
If the seven grasping at a self are not called "bondage by signs," how can the six consciousnesses be called "bondage by signs"? Furthermore, this treatise states:
"As for what is called 'bondage by signs'..."

This means that because one cannot comprehend the characteristics of objects as being like illusions and so forth, the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) is constrained by the image-part (nimitta-bhāga) and lacks autonomy; therefore, it is called "bondage by characteristics" (lakṣaṇa-bandhana).

For this reason, it is known that [the binding of appearances] applies to all eight consciousnesses. Question: If that were so, then for those in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) among the two vehicles, there would have to be the binding of appearances within the fifth and eighth consciousnesses, because they do not fully understand them as illusions.
Answer: There are two interpretations.
The first view holds that because the defiled mind (*kliṣṭamanas*) has ceased, the five [sense-consciousnesses] and the eighth [storehouse consciousness] are without bondage.
The second view holds that since they take as their object the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) produced by out-flowing (*sāsrava*) states,
these are conceptualized aspects and thus constitute the bondage of signs (*nimittabandhana*).

Just as the outflows (*āsrava*) were previously established as outflows because they were associated with the seventh [consciousness], so too the seven defiled [consciousnesses]—at times five and at other times eight—are still comprised within the outflows. The same should apply to the bondage of characteristics (*nimitta-bandhana*).
Question: Regarding the bondage of characteristics, it is said that the characteristic itself is called the "bondage of names" (*nāma-bandhana*) when it pertains to the views (*dṛṣṭi*).
The view-bondage that is self-realized is called "view-bondage," etc. Answer: As explained in the *Juyao jie* (Essential Explanation), it is also admitted that this is called a "bondage.
Some say: "That which is of the same kind is not a bondage; that which is of a different kind constitutes bondage. The *Yaoji* (Essential Collection) states:
Now, it is said that because the three wheels (trimaṇḍala) perceived by vision are not like illusions and so forth, they are called "bonds of characteristics" (lakṣaṇabandha).
Other parts are not like this, and therefore they are not called bonds.
Some say this contradicts the text.
However, because the characteristics [of the objects] such as giving are not lost,
some say this contradicts reason;
for [they argue that] when seeds produce fruits, there must be a distinction between the capacity [to act] and the object of cognition.
How can it be that you do not permit the teaching of the bound and the binding? Now, I say that your collection of arguments contradicts itself from beginning to end.
Why? It is difficult to find a statement that does not contradict the text;
yet you claim it contradicts the text, when the text merely states that giving and so forth do not lose their characteristics.
This means that it is not permitted for other factors to be designated as "bondage.
An objection may be raised: "Because they are precisely the subject and object of cognition (*ālambana*).
If one were to allow that the subject and object of cognition constitute bondage, [then the following would follow].
The previous objection was that the three wheels are not [the bondage].
If only the three wheels were called bondage,
then it would be incorrect for both the agent and the object to be bound.
If it is said that "it is difficult to find" based on the explanation of bondage by way of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*),
and if it is further argued that "it is difficult to find" based on the explanation of bondage by way of the grasper and the grasped (*ālambana*),
then would it not follow that the bondage of the grasper and the grasped is itself not bondage?
Since you yourself have already conceded that [the self] is bound, how can you raise this objection?

Some say that the treatise’s discussion of the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala*) is based on an exposition intended for easy understanding. Furthermore, the treatise states that there are many kinds of bondage.
Alternatively, two types of bondage are taught:
first, bondage by association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*),
and second, bondage by object (*ālambana-bandhana*).
Furthermore, two kinds of bondage are taught:
first, the bondage of the subject that perceives;
second, the bondage of the object perceived.
Furthermore, two types of bondage are taught:
first, the bondage of signs (nimitta-bandhana);

second, the bondage of coarse heaviness (dauṣṭhulya-bandhana). These cause the sovereign subject that takes objects as its support, along with its objects, to be unable to attain mastery either simultaneously or sequentially.
Because they are bound by associated phenomena (*saṃprayukta-dharma*), "association" is designated as a "binding" based on its function;

thus, it is called the "bond of association. Because they are constrained by the object that serves as the domain for the sovereign cognizer (*ālambaka-rāja*), it is called the "bond of the object-condition" (*ālambana-bandhana*).
Regarding the statement that "the mind that clings to phenomena as real is the binding subject":
this means that the object which is bound serves as the binding subject for the mind that takes it as its cognitive object.
This is analogous to the name *ālaya-vijñāna* (storehouse consciousness). Regarding "bondage by signs" (*nimitta-bandhana*): [it refers to the bondage arising from the objective appearances].
When the mind is constrained by characteristics (*nimitta*), it is called "bondage by characteristics" (*nimittabandhana*). There are three [types] of bondage by characteristics.
One school asserts that all objective aspects (*nimittabhāga*) are termed "bondage";
this is the position of Master Sthiramati.
According to the explanation based on the adherence to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), because there is the grasped and the grasper,
even though one knows [phenomena] to be like an illusion, one cannot be without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Alternatively, this is consistent with Dharmapāla’s position, which relies on the fact that [beings] do not realize [phenomena] are like illusions due to their clinging to a self (*ātma-grāha*), rather than relying on their clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).
Furthermore, it is said: "As long as this mental faculty (*manas*) has not been extinguished, the consciousnesses will never be liberated from bondage."

The third [position] holds that since there is no manas, there is no bondage of signs; the second [position] holds that only tainted signs are called the bondage of signs, excluding only the untainted [signs], which pertain to all eight consciousnesses.
One interpretation states that this refers to the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), because one fails to realize they are illusory and thus clings to them as being real.

Another interpretation states that this refers to the attachment to a self (*ātman-grāha*); since failing to realize they are illusory constitutes a bondage by signs (*nimittabandhana*), it encompasses the attachment to phenomena as well.
If one does not understand that illusions are like illusions, one is bound within birth and death;
this is called "bondage by signs" (*nimitta-bandhana*), which resides solely in self-grasping.
Third, according to the practice of the six perfections, it refers to the signs of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*).

However, regarding the objective aspect associated with the sixth consciousness that is conjoined with the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*), one cannot thereby achieve the perfection (*pāramitā*). If that were so, then all wholesome minds would be devoid of the grasping of a self.
The practice of the perfections is wholesome.

It should be without the bonds of signs. Answer: Based on the explanation of their intermingling, one cannot eliminate signs. Question: If there is no self, then that very intermingling is called signlessness.
What is the distinction between the supremacy of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) and the supremacy of purity (*viśuddhi*)? Answer: Skillful means is based on non-grasping (*anupādāna*);
purity is based on freedom from regret (*avipratisāra*).
All explanations regarding the bonds of characteristics (*lakṣaṇabandhana*) do not exceed these two. As for the bond of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulyabandhana*), it is as follows:
In summary, there are four types of *dausthulya* (gross heaviness) that encompass all textual accounts.
First, the manifest outflows (*āsrava*) of all minds and mental factors;
these correspond to the twenty-four *dausthulyas* described in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.
1. The two obstacles in their active manifestation; 2.
the seeds of the two obstacles; 3.
the habitual tendencies of the two obstacles.
This may be so. Just as it is commonly taught that manifest mental factors are associated with outflows and possess the three natures,
the same should apply to their seeds.
Because the meaning of "coarseness" (*dauṣṭhulya*) regarding seeds that are wholesome or neutral is somewhat obscure,

it is not mentioned in the various abbreviated [treatises]. Here, however, we explain the bondage of characteristics (*lakṣaṇabandhana*) based on the influence of self-grasping (*ātmagrāha*) and as taught in the context of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
Based on the common and the uncommon,
it is taught in terms of self-clinging in contrast to the Lesser Vehicle;
based on its own specific meaning, it is taught in terms of the six perfections.
Regarding what is called "coarseness" (*dauṣṭhulya*), this treatise does not explain it explicitly;
however, there is a verse from a sutra that addresses it.
As appropriate for each case, one must cultivate both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* in order to eliminate it.
The general explanation is without error,
because the term "with outflows" (sāsrava) indicates that which is associated with the outflows.
There are three types of that which is with outflows.
That which is of one essence with the outflows (*āsrava*) and possesses existence is called "with-outflow" (*sāsrava*).
Thus, among the three outflows, it is referred to as "with-outflow.
Here, "existence" (*bhava*) refers to the three realms of existence (*tribhava*).
This explains that the internal body of the higher realms is considered "existence" (bhava).
Because beings in these two upper realms give rise to craving for the body while being free from craving for external objects, it is called "outflow of existence" (āsrava of bhava).
Outflows pertaining to existence are termed "outflows of existence."
The afflictions of the two realms are called "outflows" (āsrava).
Because these outflows belong to all [beings],
and because there are outflows belonging to others, they are called "with-outflows" (sāsrava).
That is to say, it has the capacity [to produce rebirth].
Third, because they are conjoined with the nature of outflows (*āsrava*), they are called "with-outflows" (*sāsrava*);
they are also the very essence of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Because these outflows exist within the cycle of birth and death, their very essence possesses function; thus, they are called "with outflows" (*sāsrava*).

Now, in this context, that which is said to be "conjoined with outflows" refers to that which has the capacity for [the outflows] as its essence, and is thus termed "with outflows," rather than referring to the afflictions themselves.
Therefore, the previous partial objection stated:
"Furthermore, at the time of wholesome or non-obscured neutral minds,
if there were no grasping at a self, they would not be outflowing (sāsrava)."
The *Yogācārabhūmi* states that [a phenomenon] is "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) solely because it possesses the outflows of others.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, however, explains this comprehensively. Question:

If something is established as "with outflows" only when it is concomitant with the outflows themselves, then this would contradict both the third chapter of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and the sixty-fifth [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
In those two treatises, that which is associated with outflows (*āsrava*) is not the only thing designated as "with outflows" (*sāsrava*). How so? First, regarding the *Abhidharma*, it states:
"Because they are the intrinsic nature of the outflows;
because they are connected to the outflows."
Because they are bound by the outflows,
because they are accompanied by the outflows,
and because they conform to the outflows.
Because they belong to the category of outflows (*āsrava*), and because their primary nature is that of an outflow, they are the very essence of affliction (*kleśa*).
Because they are conjoined with the nature of an outflow, they are called "with-outflow" (*sāsrava*).
Thus, because these entities themselves involve outflows within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), they are termed "conjoined with the nature of an outflow."
The remaining five types are called "with outflows" (sāsrava) by virtue of this intrinsic nature. Regarding the connection with outflows:
that which is associated with outflows and that which is the basis for outflows—namely, defiled mind and mental factors—is what is termed "associated."

The universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*), the object-specific factors (*viniyata*), and those associated with the first seven consciousnesses—along with the five sense organs such as the eye—are called the "basis of the outflows" (*āśraya*).
As for that which is "bound," it refers to contaminated wholesome phenomena (*sāsrava-kuśala-dharma*).
Because the power of the outflows (*āsrava*) brings about future existence, this also includes the six external objects and the indeterminate mind.
This is stated according to the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*; however, if one follows the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*:
Past and future untainted dharmas, as well as wholesome and neutral minds, are all not bound;
furthermore, external objects of the present that are not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) are also not bound.
This is stated according to their substantial nature.
Because the past and future do not exist [as substantial entities],
wholesome and indeterminate minds are not associated with the outflows (*āsrava*).
This is because when an outflowing mind takes them as objects, those objects exist in the past or the future.

If manifest form were not an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) because the mind does not directly apprehend the substance (*dravya*), it would follow that it is not an object-condition (*ālambana*). However, according to the *Abhidharmakośa*, it is established as an object-condition by way of the direct image-part (*nimittabhāga*) and the indirect object-condition.
The same as [section] sixty-six.
This is an explanation regarding the severance of the bonds of conditions;
since each is based on a single specific meaning, there is no contradiction. "That which is followed by outflows" (āsrava-anuśayita).
This refers to the dharmas of other stages,
because they do not mutually augment one another.
Regarding "conducive to outflows" (āsrava-anuloma):
Regarding the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*):
they do not increase when in a different stage (*bhūmi*), but they do increase when in the same stage.
Because it is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*).
If it were without outflows (*anāsrava*), it would not be conducive [to liberation].
Although that which possesses outflows increases the turning away from existence (*bhava*), [it does so] because it is associated with outflows.
However, it coexists with the outflows (*āsrava*).
It is not otherwise, for it is neither the outflow itself nor the basis for designating the outflow.
Alternatively, although it coexists with the outflows, it does not increase them.
It is so called because it turns by diminishing power and augmenting capacity.
However, the statement that it "becomes outflowing" (sāsrava) refers to the augmentation of other outflows.
As for the category of outflows (āsrava-jāti):
The aggregates of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) arise from afflictions produced in previous lives; thus,
the *Yogācārabhūmi* (65) explains the distinctions of the contaminated (sāsrava).
It is by way of five aspects:
namely, by way of the entity (*vastu*), the latent disposition (*anuśaya*), the association (*samprayoga*), the object (*ālambana*), and the manifestation (*samutthāna*).
The "entity" refers to pure matter and the three natures of mind and mental factors.
This is the entity that possesses the nature of the outflows (*āsrava*).
It is designated as "with outflow" (*sāsrava*) according to its respective application by means of four other characteristics:
namely, by way of latent tendency (*anuśaya*), association (*samprayoga*), object (*ālambana*), and arising (*samudācāra*).
The seeds of all those aforementioned phenomena whose afflictions have not yet been severed are called *anuśaya*.
Because of these seeds, they are said to be "with outflows" (*sāsrava*).
All defiled minds and mental factors are said to be "with outflows" by virtue of their association (*saṃprayoga*) with them.
If all things that exist are the objects of direct perception,
or if they arise through the predominant influence of what is outflowing (sāsrava),
then all such things are called "outflowing" because they are the objective conditions for outflows.
The present is called "possessing an object.

If consciousness, based on pure form (*rūpa*), operates upon it, this is called the domain of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). This is based on the fact that greed and other afflictions can directly perceive objects such as those forms; thus, they are termed "objects of outflow" (*āsrava-ālambana*).
The others are not objects of perception (*ālambana*).
The treatise states: "Afflictions arise solely from the signs (*nimitta*) produced by one's own conceptualization (*vikalpa*);
it is not because those phenomena serve as clearly manifest objects of activity for them."
Therefore, as in the previous assembly, they become tainted (sāsrava) due to their arising;
this is because the latent dispositions (anuśaya) have not been abandoned and objects conducive to affliction (kleśa) manifest before them.
This is based on the induction by delusion. Furthermore, it says:
From all unwholesome afflictions,
various ripened fruits,
and the external objects produced by the predominance of those ripened fruits, [arising occurs].
Because they also arise [from them], they are called "with outflows" (*sāsrava*).

That which arises depending on these fruits of the outflows is also called "with outflows. Among the five aggregates of phenomena in their state of being with outflows, within the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), [the following applies].

According to the *Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā* (Section 6) and the *Yogācārabhūmi* (Section 5), how many meanings does each [of the categories] possess that are designated as "outflow-tainted" (*sāsrava*)?
This is as explained in the lower volume of the *Zhuyao*, in the analysis of the three types of abandonment regarding the twelve links of dependent origination.

Based on these two passages, it is not only that which is associated with outflows (*āsrava*) that is termed "with outflows" (*sāsrava*). Answer: This [definition] relies on the primary cause (*nidāna*), whereas the other relies on a specific meaning (*viśeṣārtha*).
Therefore, there is no contradiction.
Regarding the statement that they mutually augment one another:
it is asked whether the seventh [consciousness] serves as the basis for the defilement of the sixth, thereby augmenting the sixth.
How do the six consciousnesses augment the seventh? Answer:
There are two meanings. First, increase;
second, non-diminution. If the sixth consciousness initiates karma and induces the eighth [consciousness], it serves as its support and condition.
It is called "augmentation" (anuśaya) because it continues in a continuous succession; even when arising as outflow-tainted (sāsrava),
although it may not increase the seventh [consciousness],
it is still called "augmentation" because it does not harm it.
It is not like the arising of the untainted (anāsrava), which necessarily diminishes that [defilement] and is thus not called "increase";
nor is it like sleep, which,
although it cannot increase the faculty of the eye, [is still not considered an increase].
That which does not cause harm is also called "nourishing" (āpyāyana);
this case should be understood in the same way.
This explains how the name of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is derived.
Question: Since both the fifth and eighth [consciousnesses] rely upon the seventh,
why is the sixth called the "unshared basis" (*asādhāraṇa-āśraya*),
and why does it alone receive the name "mental consciousness" (*mano-vijñāna*) rather than the fifth or eighth?

Answer: If one considers the basis for defilement and purification as well as the co-existent basis (*sahabhū-āśraya*), then both the seventh and the eighth [consciousnesses] serve as the bases for the [first] five.
However, regarding that which is the immediate, conforming, and uncommon basis (*āsanna-anukūla-asādhāraṇa-āśraya*):
That is to say, it belongs exclusively to the sixth [consciousness].
The present mention of the "unshared mind" (asādhāraṇa-manas) indicates that which is proximate and conducive to arising.
Why is this? Because the six seeds necessarily follow the seven kinds [of consciousness], and the seven kinds give rise to the manifest mental consciousness as they arise.
This is like the seed of visual consciousness depending upon the seed of the eye-faculty.
This case is also like that.

Because the five [bases] and the eight [liberations] do not mention the seventh kind as their support, it is therefore named "without confusion. If that is so, why are the seven supports and the eight births not called "mind"?

Question: Why is the eighth [consciousness], which relies on the seven births, not called "mind" (*manas*)? Answer: The *Śāstra* states that it receives the name "mind" (*citta*) because it discerns; this does not apply to the "intellect" (*manas*).
Furthermore, while the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses] are each their own continuous stream, [the others are not].
It receives its name from its essential nature.
Since the six consciousnesses are intermittent,
it is named after its basis and its objects.
Alternatively, based on the boundaries and locations, both are termed "mind-intellect" (manas-citta).
The seventh is called "mind-intellect," while the eighth is called "intellect-mind" (citta-manas).
In principle, there is no error;
however, there is no explicit textual authority for this.
Discourse.
Regarding the statement that if one attains mastery, the sense faculties function interchangeably,
there are two explanations for this essential point.
Within the first master's view, there are further two interpretations.
One interpretation states that each of the five consciousnesses is able to take all objects as its conditions and apprehend their specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa),
without the fault of the sense organs and objects being impaired.
As for the terms "separation" and "conjunction":
This is stated from the perspective of the causal stage;

it does not obstruct the resultant stage, because [the latter] has attained mastery. Furthermore, although the eighth consciousness perceives all objects and grasps their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), [it does not grasp their general characteristics].
There is no fault of destruction,
because at the stage of fruition the essence possesses multiple capacities;
it is not that the essence undergoes transformation into the essence of another phenomenon.
One must not object by saying that what sees form is called the eye,
yet one also allows that what hears sound and so forth is [the ear]; furthermore,
that which acts as the creator is called the "great" (mahābhūta).
Form and so forth are also capable of producing;
that their essence undergoes transformation is this functional capacity.
If one were to see by means of form,
it could be analogized to form being able to create;
[yet] seeing form is the function of the eye.
This is not a transformation of the substance (*svabhāva*).
However, the Master’s intention lies in the second interpretation.
According to the second teacher, each [faculty] returns to its own root and perceives its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is not called "mutual functioning. The *Yāoyí* says:
According to ancient tradition, there were three masters.
One said that a single consciousness universally relies upon the six sense organs,
each apprehending its own respective object obtained by that organ.
Second, it is said that a single consciousness universally takes the six objects as its conditions,
each relying on its own respective sense organ;
this is because the objects are common [to all].
The inferior [view] holds that it is common to others;
one school says that a single consciousness is commonly based upon the six sense organs and commonly takes the six objects as its conditions.
This has not yet been definitively resolved.
The faculties and consciousnesses are not shared;
the objects are what are shared.
One does not wish to destroy that which is the domain of one's own faculties and consciousness.
If a single consciousness were to depend upon all the sense organs simultaneously,
it would undermine the distinction between the organs and the consciousness;
therefore, it perceives other objects by means of its own respective organ rather than another's.
"Existing now, yet not fully understood"—this "now" refers to that which remains.
Why? Because the object is a common apprehension;
it is inherently established as common. If one does not wish to destroy the domain traversed by one's own faculties and consciousness, [one must acknowledge this].
Since the universal [cognitions] depend upon the various sense-faculties, they are immediately destroyed along with those faculties and consciousnesses.
Therefore, while one faculty employs its own object and does not employ another faculty, the present [consciousness] relies on its own faculty to apprehend other objects;
it does not distinguish between separation and union, and it apprehends both conventional and ultimate objects.
Is it not the case that there would still be the fault of the destruction of the faculties and their objects?
For other consciousnesses and faculties would then be apprehending other objects.
Since this has not been explained away.
One should rely on the essential points.
Question: Are the five consciousnesses produced determinately when they take the objects of the five sensory realms as their conditions?
If they are produced determinately, they should be subsumed under the *dharmāyatana*.
The five faculties are also like this. Answer: There are two interpretations.
According to the tenth [chapter] below, one says they are the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
This is because only the three realms constitute the outflow-free (*anāsrava*).
One interpretation states: that which is transformed by meditative concentration (*samādhi*) does not necessarily fall within the category of the *dharmāyatana*.
If it arises through the power of concentration in the formless realms, it is subsumed under the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*),
because there is no distinction between the supporting faculty and its object.
If it arises through the power of supernormal powers in the form realms, [it is likewise subsumed under the sphere of phenomena].
They are generally subsumed under their own respective bases (*āyatana*).

For example, the divine eye and ear are not included within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). Alternatively, when they rely on a physical basis (*dravya*), they are subsumed among the five sense objects (*viṣaya*);
however, when they arise as mere mental images (*pratibimba*), they are subsumed within the base of mental objects.
Alternatively, those that are naturally uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) in the state of a Buddha are included within the objects of the five sense-fields;
those newly perfumed are subsumed under the sphere of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*),
because they are natural and do not arise through meditative concentration or supernormal powers.
If it is newly perfumed, it arises through meditative concentration and supernormal powers.
Regarding the question of whether the five consciousnesses can be admitted to coexist with all three moral natures:
for instance, once a wholesome visual consciousness has reached its state of outflow (*nisyanda*).
When an unwholesome ear-consciousness takes an object and,
through that contact, gives rise to a sudden, impulsive mind (*saṃhatābhinirhāra-citta*),
at that time the mental consciousness likewise hears the sound.
Is this a spontaneous mind (*āveṇika*) or an outflowing mind (*naiṣyandika*)?
If it were an outflowing mind, it would have to be of the same wholesome nature as the visual consciousness.
Spontaneous indeterminate [states] and the three types of indeterminate [states] prior to the transformation of the basis cannot coexist within a single moment of mind as two distinct natures.
If it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), how can the visual consciousness at that time become wholesome?
[Is it not because] a wholesome mental consciousness acts as the inducer? Answer: For now, let us address the first objection.
Regarding the meaning of the five types of consciousness:
the wholesome resultant mind shares the same object as the ear-consciousness;
although it is of a wholesome nature, [it is not so in its arising].
It is also called "sudden" (saurer),
because the object of sound has newly fallen upon the mind;
it cannot be said to be a mind of outflow (niṣyanda).
Because the sound has not been previously heard,
it cannot be merely a sudden encounter;
furthermore, it shares the same object of cognition as the visual consciousness.
Therefore, the cause is common to both [the wholesome and the unwholesome],
yet it is of a wholesome nature.
As for the statement that the first three minds, in the stage prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*):
Alternatively, this is explained from the perspective of those who have not yet fully transformed their basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) and lack mastery over the five distinct types of mind;
it is stated as a general rule.
For one who has already attained the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti),
who has obtained mastery,
and who is endowed with the five minds:
It can be explained as pertaining to all three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
Otherwise, how could the treatise state: "When perceiving a sound, one does not immediately emerge from meditative absorption;
rather, having perceived the sound, if there is a subsequent aspiration, only then does one emerge"?
This statement that "expectation" (*āśā*) is the mind of seeking means that one cannot say that one emerges from meditative absorption at the very moment of desiring or expecting it.
The treatise states: "If there is expectation, one subsequently emerges from absorption. Thus, it is not the case that one emerges immediately upon the arising of desire.

Nor can it be said that one establishes a formal vow during the preliminary practice beforehand, thinking, "If I hear a different sound, I shall immediately emerge from meditative absorption to seek out the object"; thus, it is called "aspiration."
One does not engage in seeking while in meditative concentration.
At what time is there the expectation of sound?
Is it within the state of concentration?
This refers to having already emerged from meditative absorption;
if one were still within absorption,
the mind of aspiration would itself constitute seeking.
Because the mind of seeking is accompanied by desire (*chanda*).
If this aspiration were not seeking,
under which mental factor would it be subsumed?
If it were said that one has already emerged from meditative absorption (*vyutthita*) upon having a hope or expectation, this would contradict the treatise.
The treatise states: "If there is a hope or expectation, one emerges only at a later time. Ximing’s commentary says:
If one relies on the original text, it is not the case that the mental consciousness associated with that very meditative absorption can apprehend this sound;
thus, the two interpretations offered by the commentators differ. Now, I maintain that this is not so.
Because it contradicts the treatise,
the cited commentary is neither a sūtra nor a śāstra and thus cannot serve as proof.
Regarding the resolution of the subsequent objection:
The treatise states that the five consciousnesses are induced to become wholesome or defiled by the mental consciousness;
this is said with reference to their initial arising,
not in terms of their continuous state, for at the time they persist as wholesome or defiled, they are not always induced by the mental consciousness.
Therefore, the treatise below states:
"In various places, it is only said that the mental consciousness associated with the five [sensory consciousnesses] also takes the five objects as its objects;
it does not say they are of the same nature. Ximing says:
Only the three types of mind—sudden (ābhoga), defiled (kliṣṭa), pure (śuddha), and outflowing (naiṣyandika)—are associated with the five sensory consciousnesses.
The seeking (paryeṣaka) and determining (niścaya) minds exclusively take the past as their object through inference (anumāna).
It does not coexist with the five [sensory consciousnesses].

Question: As stated previously in the fourth [section], when encountering an object that is not superior, it may be granted that the five consciousnesses are interrupted following a *saurer* (sudden/arbitrary) mind.
When encountering a superior object, the five [cognitions] arise spontaneously;

yet, how could it be that they do not subsequently arise without interruption as subsequent investigation, ascertainment, defiled, or pure outflowing cognitions? Furthermore, is it not the case that after the arising of seeking, one only then gives rise to ascertainment, the defiled, or the outflowing?
If there is investigation and decision (*vitarka-vicāra*),
why do they not coexist with the five sensory consciousnesses?
The explanation is that although the state of encountering a superior object may last for many moments, [the five consciousnesses lack these mental factors].
If it arises abruptly and is not interrupted,
yet there is no other mind [present],
then such an abrupt arising would be exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta).
If the realm of the gods of wrath were indeed a superior state,
